rules.title: App Transport Security is turned off
rules.why: NSAllowsArbitraryLoads turns ATS off for the whole app; NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsInWebContent turns it off for everything web views load. Anyone on the same network, such as public Wi-Fi, can then read and change plain HTTP traffic, including tokens and personal data.
rules.fix: Remove NSAllowsArbitraryLoads and NSAllowsArbitraryLoadsInWebContent from Info.plist (and any INFOPLIST_KEY_ build setting that adds them). If one host really needs HTTP, add a narrow NSExceptionDomains entry for that host only.
rules.verify: Build the release configuration, open an http:// URL your app uses, and confirm the request fails with an App Transport Security error.

fix_code.code:
<key>NSAppTransportSecurity</key>
<dict>
    <!-- No NSAllowsArbitraryLoads: ATS blocks plain HTTP and requires TLS 1.2+. -->
    <!-- Only if one host truly needs HTTP: -->
    <!--
    <key>NSExceptionDomains</key>
    <dict>
        <key>legacy.example.com</key>
        <dict>
            <key>NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads</key>
            <true/>
        </dict>
    </dict>
    -->
</dict>

rules.title: An ATS exception allows plain HTTP to a host
rules.why: NSExceptionAllowsInsecureHTTPLoads lets the app talk to that host over plain HTTP. Anyone on the network path can read or change those requests and responses.
rules.fix: Move the host to HTTPS and delete the exception. If you can't yet, keep the exception to that one host, without NSIncludesSubdomains, and plan its removal.
rules.verify: Remove the exception, build the release configuration, and confirm every request to that host still works over https://.

rules.title: A TLS version below 1.2 is allowed
rules.why: ATS requires at least TLS 1.2. An NSExceptionMinimumTLSVersion of TLSv1.0 or TLSv1.1, or a URLSession minimum set that low, lets a connection fall back to old protocol versions with known weaknesses.
rules.fix: Delete the NSExceptionMinimumTLSVersion entry (ATS then enforces TLS 1.2), and set tlsMinimumSupportedProtocolVersion to .TLSv12 or higher in code.
rules.verify: Point a test build at a server limited to TLS 1.1 (for example `openssl s_server -accept 8443 -tls1_1 -cipher 'DEFAULT:@SECLEVEL=0' -cert cert.pem -key key.pem` behind a test hostname) and confirm the app refuses the connection.

rules.title: A server-trust handler accepts certificates without validating them
rules.why: The authentication-challenge handler returns .useCredential for the server's trust without calling SecTrustEvaluateWithError. An attacker on the network can present any certificate, even a self-signed one, and read or change all traffic.
rules.fix: Validate the chain with SecTrustEvaluateWithError before anything else, cancel the challenge when it fails, and only then compare pins. If you don't pin, return .performDefaultHandling.
rules.verify: Route the app through a proxy whose CA the device does not trust (mitmproxy, §22.3) and confirm every request fails with a TLS error.

rules.title: Pinning code falls back to default handling when no pin matches
rules.why: The delegate compares pins but never cancels the challenge. When no pin matches it returns .performDefaultHandling, which accepts any publicly trusted certificate, so the pinning check never blocks anything.
rules.fix: Return .cancelAuthenticationChallenge when the chain fails validation and when no pin matches. Use .performDefaultHandling only for challenges that aren't server trust.
rules.verify: Make the pin set wrong in a test build and confirm requests fail with NSURLErrorCancelled (-999), as in §8.10.

rules.title: Pinned domain has no backup pin
rules.why: NSPinnedDomains pins never expire. With a single pin, a key rotation or a CA change locks every user on that build out of your servers until they install an update.
rules.fix: Add a second SPKI-SHA256-BASE64 entry: a backup key at a second CA, or a key you hold offline. If you list both CA and leaf identities, each list needs its own backup. With react-native-ssl-public-key-pinning, list two or more `publicKeyHashes` for each host.
rules.verify: Serve a test endpoint with a certificate issued for the backup key (or from the backup CA) and confirm the app connects. Then confirm that a certificate matching neither pin fails.
rules.not_needed_reason: Your app type usually doesn't need pinning (§8.8). If you keep the pins anyway, add a backup pin so a key change can't lock users out.

fix_code.code:
<key>NSAppTransportSecurity</key>
<dict>
    <key>NSPinnedDomains</key>
    <dict>
        <key>api.example.com</key>
        <dict>
            <key>NSIncludesSubdomains</key>
            <true/>
            <!-- Pins an intermediate or root. Use NSPinnedLeafIdentities to pin the leaf. -->
            <key>NSPinnedCAIdentities</key>
            <array>
                <dict>
                    <key>SPKI-SHA256-BASE64</key>
                    <string>YLh1dUR9y6Kja30RrAn7JKnbQG/uEtLMkBgFF2Fuihg=</string>
                </dict>
                <dict>
                    <!-- Backup pin -->
                    <key>SPKI-SHA256-BASE64</key>
                    <string>Vjs8r4z+80wjNcr1YKepWQboSIRi63WsWXhIMN+eWys=</string>
                </dict>
            </array>
        </dict>
    </dict>
</dict>

rules.title: No certificate pinning (needed for high-risk apps)
rules.why: Without pinning, any certificate from a CA the device trusts is accepted, including a root installed through a configuration profile or MDM. For money and health data, the book recommends SPKI pinning on an intermediate with a backup.
rules.fix: Pin the SPKI of your intermediate CA with NSPinnedDomains (simplest) or a URLSessionDelegate that validates first, plus a backup pin and a written rotation runbook. Pin only if you can also run failure alerts, CT monitoring, and a protected kill switch (§8.7); if not, don't pin and rely on strict TLS plus CT (§8.9). In React Native, call `initializeSslPinning` (react-native-ssl-public-key-pinning) before the first request.
rules.verify: Make the device trust a proxy CA, then confirm requests to pinned hosts fail while an unpinned host still loads through the proxy (§8.10, step 1).
rules.not_needed_reason: Book §8.8: outside banking, health, identity, and apps that handle card numbers, strict TLS plus Certificate Transparency monitoring is a reasonable position, and pinning adds operational risk. Enterprise apps: trust your private CA explicitly instead (§8.8).

fix_code.code:
<key>NSAppTransportSecurity</key>
<dict>
    <key>NSPinnedDomains</key>
    <dict>
        <key>api.example.com</key>
        <dict>
            <key>NSIncludesSubdomains</key>
            <true/>
            <!-- Pins an intermediate or root. Use NSPinnedLeafIdentities to pin the leaf. -->
            <key>NSPinnedCAIdentities</key>
            <array>
                <dict>
                    <key>SPKI-SHA256-BASE64</key>
                    <string>YLh1dUR9y6Kja30RrAn7JKnbQG/uEtLMkBgFF2Fuihg=</string>
                </dict>
                <dict>
                    <!-- Backup pin -->
                    <key>SPKI-SHA256-BASE64</key>
                    <string>Vjs8r4z+80wjNcr1YKepWQboSIRi63WsWXhIMN+eWys=</string>
                </dict>
            </array>
        </dict>
    </dict>
</dict>

rules.title: Keychain item is readable before the first unlock
rules.why: kSecAttrAccessibleAlways (and AlwaysThisDeviceOnly) makes the item readable even before the user first unlocks the phone. These are the items forensic tools recover from a locked device. Apple deprecated the class in iOS 12.
rules.fix: Use kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly. If background work needs the item while the phone is locked, use kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly. In React Native, use ACCESSIBLE.WHEN_UNLOCKED_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY (react-native-keychain) or SecureStore.WHEN_UNLOCKED_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY (expo-secure-store).
rules.verify: Search the code for kSecAttrAccessibleAlways and confirm no match. On a test device, lock it and confirm background code that needs the item behaves as you expect.

rules.title: Keychain item can migrate to another device
rules.why: Without ThisDeviceOnly, the item can be restored from a backup onto another device. A session token then travels with the backup instead of staying on the phone it was issued to. KeychainAccess defaults to .afterFirstUnlock, which has the same problem.
rules.fix: Append ThisDeviceOnly: kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly, or AfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly for items that background work needs. With KeychainAccess, call .accessibility(.whenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly). Skip this for items you sync on purpose with kSecAttrSynchronizable. In React Native, pass `accessible: ACCESSIBLE.WHEN_UNLOCKED_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY` to react-native-keychain (its default is AFTER_FIRST_UNLOCK) and `keychainAccessible: SecureStore.WHEN_UNLOCKED_THIS_DEVICE_ONLY` to expo-secure-store (its default is WHEN_UNLOCKED).
rules.verify: Back up a test device, restore it onto a second device, and confirm the app asks the user to sign in again.

rules.title: File written with no Data Protection
rules.why: NSFileProtectionNone (.noFileProtection) leaves the file readable at all times, even before the first unlock after a restart. Anyone who extracts data from the device can read it.
rules.fix: Write sensitive files with .completeFileProtection, and exclude them from backup. Use completeUntilFirstUserAuthentication only for files background work must read while locked. Never set the com.apple.developer.default-data-protection entitlement to NSFileProtectionNone.
rules.verify: On a physical device, write the file, lock the phone, and confirm code that runs while locked can't read it (the simulator doesn't enforce Data Protection).

rules.title: Token or password stored in UserDefaults
rules.why: UserDefaults is a plain plist in the app container (or in the shared App Group container for UserDefaults(suiteName:)). It is copied into backups and is readable by anyone with access to the device's files. A long-lived token there can be lifted and replayed.
rules.fix: Keep short-lived tokens in memory. Store long-lived tokens and credentials in the Keychain with kSecAttrAccessibleWhenUnlockedThisDeviceOnly. Leave only non-secret settings in UserDefaults.
rules.verify: On the simulator, sign in, then run `grep -rl "eyJ" "$(xcrun simctl get_app_container booted <bundle id> data)/Library/Preferences"` and confirm there is no output. UserDefaults is a binary plist, so don't add `-I`. If your tokens aren't JWTs, search for a known part of one instead.

rules.title: Biometric check only flips a boolean
rules.why: LAContext.evaluatePolicy returns a success flag. An attacker with Frida calls your success branch without any Face ID or Touch ID happening, and the bypass takes minutes. Nothing cryptographic depends on the result.
rules.fix: Bind the prompt to a key: create a Secure Enclave key with SecAccessControl [.privateKeyUsage, .biometryCurrentSet] and sign a server challenge with it. The server accepts the action only with a valid signature.
rules.verify: Hook evaluatePolicy to report success (for example, `ios ui biometrics_bypass` in objection) and confirm the protected action still fails because no valid signature reaches the server.

rules.title: Biometric key stays valid after a new fingerprint or face is enrolled
rules.why: With .biometryAny, someone who knows the device passcode can enroll their own fingerprint or face and then unlock your app's protected key. .biometryCurrentSet invalidates the key when the enrolled set changes.
rules.fix: Replace .biometryAny with .biometryCurrentSet, and handle the signing failure that follows an enrollment change by sending the user to re-enroll or to server-side step-up.
rules.verify: Add a new fingerprint or re-enroll Face ID on a test device, use the feature again, and confirm signing fails and the app asks the user to re-enroll.

pattern.message: This access control accepts any enrolled biometric, including one added later.

rules.title: Web view inspection is on in release builds
rules.why: isInspectable = true lets anyone with the device and a Mac attach Safari's Web Inspector, read the page, and call your JavaScript bridge from a console.
rules.fix: Wrap the line in #if DEBUG so it never compiles into release builds. In React Native, pass `webviewDebuggingEnabled={__DEV__}`.
rules.verify: Install the release build on a device connected to a Mac, open a web view screen, and confirm your app doesn't appear in Safari's Develop menu.

fix_code.code:
let webView = WKWebView(frame: .zero, configuration: config)
#if DEBUG
if #available(iOS 16.4, *) { webView.isInspectable = true }   // never in release
#endif

rules.title: Script message handler doesn't check who sent the message
rules.why: WebKit has no origin allowlist for message handlers. Without a check on message.frameInfo, any page or iframe the web view loads, including an ad or an attacker's page, can call your native code.
rules.fix: In the handler, reject messages unless frameInfo.isMainFrame is true and frameInfo.securityOrigin is your https host. Then validate every argument, and let the server authorize the action.
rules.verify: Load a page from a different origin in the same web view, post a message to each handler name, and confirm every handler rejects it.

rules.title: UIWebView is still in the app
rules.why: Apple deprecated UIWebView in iOS 12 and the App Store rejects apps and updates that use it. It also runs web content inside your app's process, unlike WKWebView.
rules.fix: Replace UIWebView with WKWebView. If the reference comes from a third-party SDK, update or remove that SDK.
rules.verify: Run `grep -r UIWebView` on the source and `nm -u` on the release binary, and confirm neither finds it.

rules.title: Sign-in callback uses a custom URL scheme
rules.why: A custom URL scheme isn't tied to your app. When the redirect goes through the OS (a scheme in CFBundleURLTypes), another app that registers it can receive the authorization code. Even inside ASWebAuthenticationSession, any app can start a sign-in with your client ID and scheme and impersonate your app. A verified https callback ties the redirect to your associated domain.
rules.fix: Return to a verified https redirect: Universal Links (Associated Domains applinks:) and, on iOS 17.4+, ASWebAuthenticationSession with .https(host:path:). Keep PKCE and state either way.
rules.verify: Install a test app that registers the same scheme, start sign-in, and confirm the callback can't reach it once the https redirect is in place.

rules.title: Insecure NSKeyedUnarchiver API
rules.why: unarchiveObject(with:) and unarchiveTopLevelObjectWithData build whatever classes the archive names. If an attacker controls the bytes (a file, a deep link, a shared item), they choose which objects your app constructs.
rules.fix: Decode with Codable. If you must read NSKeyedArchiver data, use unarchivedObject(ofClass:from:) with an NSSecureCoding class.
rules.verify: Search the code for unarchiveObject(with and unarchiveTopLevelObjectWithData and confirm no match remains.

rules.title: App target has no privacy manifest
rules.why: Apple expects a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy in your app that declares collected data, tracking domains, and the reason for each required-reason API (UserDefaults is one). App Store Connect rejects uploads that use these APIs without a declared reason.
rules.fix: Add a PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy to the app target (File > New > File > App Privacy) and fill in what the app and its SDKs collect and why.
rules.verify: Archive the app, then in Xcode's Organizer choose Generate Privacy Report and confirm it lists your app's manifest.

fix_code.code:
<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>NSPrivacyTracking</key>
    <false/>
    <key>NSPrivacyTrackingDomains</key>
    <array/>
    <key>NSPrivacyCollectedDataTypes</key>
    <array/>
    <key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypes</key>
    <array>
        <dict>
            <key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPIType</key>
            <string>NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategoryUserDefaults</string>
            <key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypeReasons</key>
            <array><string>CA92.1</string></array>
        </dict>
    </array>
</dict>
</plist>

rules.title: Secret copied to the general pasteboard without localOnly
rules.why: Without .localOnly, a value on the general pasteboard can travel to the user's other Apple devices through Universal Clipboard, and other apps can read it until something replaces it.
rules.fix: Copy secrets only when the user asks, with setItems(_:options:) and the options .localOnly: true and an .expirationDate.
rules.verify: Copy the value in the app, then try pasting on a second device signed in to the same Apple Account, and confirm nothing arrives; wait past the expiration and confirm the pasteboard is empty.

fix_code.code:
import UniformTypeIdentifiers

UIPasteboard.general.setItems(
    [[UTType.plainText.identifier: sensitiveValue]],
    options: [
        .localOnly: true,                                // do not sync to other devices
        .expirationDate: Date().addingTimeInterval(60)   // clears itself
    ]
)

rules.title: Release build keeps symbols or testability
rules.why: ENABLE_TESTABILITY = YES exports internal symbols and makes Xcode skip stripping; STRIP_INSTALLED_PRODUCT = NO, STRIP_SWIFT_SYMBOLS = NO or a partial STRIP_STYLE ship the symbol table. All hand a reverse engineer readable function and type names for free.
rules.fix: In every configuration your schemes archive, set ENABLE_TESTABILITY = NO, STRIP_INSTALLED_PRODUCT = YES, STRIP_SWIFT_SYMBOLS = YES and STRIP_STYLE = all for the app, and keep symbols in a separate dSYM (DEBUG_INFORMATION_FORMAT = dwarf-with-dsym).
rules.verify: Archive the release build and run `nm -U` on the app binary: you should see few or no readable Swift or Objective-C symbol names.

fix_code.code:
// Release.xcconfig
DEPLOYMENT_POSTPROCESSING = YES
STRIP_INSTALLED_PRODUCT = YES
STRIP_STYLE = all
STRIP_SWIFT_SYMBOLS = YES
DEBUG_INFORMATION_FORMAT = dwarf-with-dsym
ENABLE_TESTABILITY = NO

rules.title: Debug tool pod or package ships in release builds
rules.why: In-app debug tools such as FLEX, netfox, Wormholy or CocoaDebug show network traffic, the view tree, files and Keychain items to whoever holds the phone. Linked into Release, they ship to every user.
rules.fix: Add :configurations => ['Debug'] to the pod, or wrap the import and setup in #if DEBUG. Swift Package Manager can't limit a package to one configuration, so guard every use.
rules.verify: Archive the Release build and run `otool -L` and `nm` on the app binary: no FLEX, netfox, Wormholy or CocoaDebug symbols should appear.

fix_code.code:
target 'MyApp' do
  # Debug-only tools never link into Release.
  pod 'FLEX', :configurations => ['Debug']
end

rules.title: Web view file-origin rules turned off through key-value coding
rules.why: allowFileAccessFromFileURLs and allowUniversalAccessFromFileURLs are private WebKit preferences. Set through setValue(_:forKey:), they let a file:// page read other local files, or any web origin, and send them anywhere.
rules.fix: Remove the setValue calls. Load bundled pages with loadFileURL(_:allowingReadAccessTo:) scoped to one folder, or serve them through a WKURLSchemeHandler.
rules.verify: Load a bundled page that tries `fetch('file:///etc/hosts')` and confirm WebKit blocks it.

rules.title: Release entitlements let a debugger attach
rules.why: get-task-allow = true lets any debugger attach to the process and read or change memory, keys and tokens. Distribution signing never sets it; a hard-coded true in a release entitlements file does.
rules.fix: Delete get-task-allow from the entitlements file. Xcode adds it for development signing only.
rules.verify: Run `codesign -d --entitlements - MyApp.app` on the archived build and confirm get-task-allow is absent or false.

rules.title: Release configuration compiles DEBUG-only code
rules.why: When a shipping configuration defines DEBUG, every #if DEBUG block (test servers, logging, bypass switches) compiles into the App Store build. It also hides those blocks from scanners that assume DEBUG is off in release.
rules.fix: Remove DEBUG from SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS, OTHER_SWIFT_FLAGS and GCC_PREPROCESSOR_DEFINITIONS in every configuration your schemes archive.
rules.verify: Run `xcodebuild -showBuildSettings -configuration Release` and confirm DEBUG isn't in SWIFT_ACTIVE_COMPILATION_CONDITIONS or GCC_PREPROCESSOR_DEFINITIONS.

rules.title: Advertising identifier read without App Tracking Transparency
rules.why: Since iOS 14.5 the IDFA may be read only after the user allows tracking in the ATT prompt, which needs a purpose string. Reading it without both breaks App Store rules and tracks people who never agreed.
rules.fix: Call ATTrackingManager.requestTrackingAuthorization before you read the IDFA, and add NSUserTrackingUsageDescription. Better, use identifierForVendor or a server-side ID.
rules.verify: Reset the simulator's privacy settings, launch the app, and confirm the ATT prompt appears before any request carries the IDFA.

fix_code.code:
import AppTrackingTransparency
import AdSupport

ATTrackingManager.requestTrackingAuthorization { status in
    guard status == .authorized else { return }   // no IDFA otherwise
    let idfa = ASIdentifierManager.shared().advertisingIdentifier
    // ...
}

rules.title: Required-reason API used without a declared reason
rules.why: UserDefaults, file timestamps, system boot time, disk space and active keyboards can fingerprint a device. Apple requires each use to be declared with an approved reason in PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy, and App Store Connect rejects uploads that don't.
rules.fix: Add an NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypes entry for the category with an approved reason code, such as CA92.1 for UserDefaults or C617.1 for file timestamps.
rules.verify: Archive the app, generate the privacy report in Xcode's Organizer, and confirm the category is listed with your reason.

fix_code.code:
<key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypes</key>
<array>
    <dict>
        <key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPIType</key>
        <string>NSPrivacyAccessedAPICategoryUserDefaults</string>
        <key>NSPrivacyAccessedAPITypeReasons</key>
        <array>
            <string>CA92.1</string>
        </array>
    </dict>
</array>

rules.title: App Attest isn't integrated
rules.why: Without App Attest, the server can't tell your genuine app from a repackaged copy, an emulator script or a bot replaying your API. DeviceCheck alone only flags devices, not the app.
rules.fix: Generate and attest a key once per install with DCAppAttestService, send an assertion with sensitive requests, and verify both on the server. In React Native, use @react-native-firebase/app-check with the App Attest provider, or react-native-device-attest.
rules.verify: Call a sensitive endpoint with curl using a valid session and confirm the server rejects it for a missing or invalid assertion.

rules.title: LocalAuthentication accepts a recent unlock
rules.why: touchIDAuthenticationAllowableReuseDuration above zero lets a device unlock from the last few seconds or minutes satisfy the check with no new prompt, so whoever picks up an unlocked phone passes it.
rules.fix: Leave touchIDAuthenticationAllowableReuseDuration at 0 for payments, transfers and other sensitive actions.
rules.verify: Unlock the device, open the sensitive action right away, and confirm Face ID or Touch ID is requested again.

rules.title: App never hides its screen in the app switcher or recordings
rules.why: iOS stores a snapshot of the last screen for the app switcher, and screen recording or mirroring shows everything live. Without an overlay, balances, messages or one-time codes stay visible there.
rules.fix: Cover sensitive views in sceneWillResignActive and remove the cover in sceneDidBecomeActive, and watch sceneCaptureState (iOS 17+) to hide content while the screen is recorded. In React Native, use expo-screen-capture or react-native-capture-protection, or cover the screen when AppState turns inactive.
rules.verify: Open a sensitive screen, swipe to the app switcher, and confirm the snapshot shows the cover; start a screen recording and confirm the content is hidden.

rules.title: Web view can read a whole app container folder
rules.why: loadFileURL(_:allowingReadAccessTo:) with Documents, Library or the home folder lets the page, and any script injected into it, read every file there: databases, caches and downloaded documents.
rules.fix: Grant read access only to the folder that holds the page, such as a subfolder of Bundle.main.resourceURL.
rules.verify: From the loaded page, try to fetch a file outside its folder (for example a database in Library) and confirm it fails.

fix_code.code:
let pageDir = Bundle.main.resourceURL!.appendingPathComponent("help", isDirectory: true)
webView.loadFileURL(pageDir.appendingPathComponent("index.html"), allowingReadAccessTo: pageDir)

rules.title: Deep link URL is loaded into a web view
rules.why: Any app or web page can open your URL scheme or universal link. If the URL it carries goes straight into a WKWebView, an attacker's page runs inside your app, next to its bridges and cookies.
rules.fix: Parse the incoming URL, require https, and compare its host with an exact allowlist before loading it. Open anything else in Safari or SFSafariViewController.
rules.verify: Run `xcrun simctl openurl booted '<scheme>://open?url=https://evil.example'` and confirm the web view doesn't load evil.example.

rules.title: Network.framework connection allows TLS below 1.2
rules.why: ATS doesn't cover Network.framework or Secure Transport connections. Allowing TLS 1.0 or 1.1 there lets an attacker on the network force a protocol with known weaknesses.
rules.fix: Set the minimum to .TLSv12 (or .TLSv13) with sec_protocol_options_set_min_tls_protocol_version.
rules.verify: Point the connection at a test server that only offers TLS 1.1 (`openssl s_server -tls1_1`) and confirm the handshake fails.

rules.title: Sensitive files sit in a Documents folder the Files app shows
rules.why: UIFileSharingEnabled exposes Documents in Finder and the Files app. Tokens, databases or exports stored there can be copied off the device by anyone with the phone, and they go into computer backups.
rules.fix: Keep app data in Application Support (or Caches), exclude it from backup where it fits, and put only files the user should see in Documents.
rules.verify: Connect the device to a Mac, open it in Finder's Files tab, and confirm no database, token or export file is listed for the app.

rules.title: Secret written to a file in the App Group container
rules.why: The App Group container is shared with every app and extension in the group and isn't Keychain-protected. A token written there as a file is as exposed as plain storage, and every member can read it.
rules.fix: Share secrets through a Keychain access group (kSecAttrAccessGroup) instead, and keep only non-secret data in the group container.
rules.verify: On a simulator, open the group container (`xcrun simctl get_app_container booted <bundle id> <group id>`) and confirm no file holds a token or password.

fix_code.code:
let query: [String: Any] = [
    kSecClass as String: kSecClassGenericPassword,
    kSecAttrAccount as String: "session",
    kSecAttrAccessGroup as String: "TEAMID.com.example.shared",   // shared with the extension
    kSecAttrAccessible as String: kSecAttrAccessibleAfterFirstUnlockThisDeviceOnly,
    kSecValueData as String: token,
]
SecItemAdd(query as CFDictionary, nil)

rules.title: App doesn't refuse third-party keyboards
rules.why: A third-party keyboard with Full Access can send everything typed into your app, including passwords and card numbers, to its developer. iOS disables custom keyboards only in secure text fields.
rules.fix: Implement application(_:shouldAllowExtensionPointIdentifier:) and return false for .keyboard. In React Native, add it to AppDelegate (bare app) or through a config plugin (Expo).
rules.verify: Install a third-party keyboard, open the app, and confirm only the system keyboard appears in every field.
rules.not_needed_reason: Refusing custom keyboards takes away the user's preferred keyboard everywhere in the app. It pays off where typed credentials and transaction details are the asset; secure text fields already use the system keyboard (§17.6).

rules.title: Bundled keyboard extension requests Full Access
rules.why: RequestsOpenAccess gives your keyboard network access and shared storage, so everything users type in any app could leave the device. Users must trust you with all their input.
rules.fix: Set RequestsOpenAccess to false unless a feature the user sees needs the network or shared storage.
rules.verify: Install the keyboard and confirm Settings doesn't offer an Allow Full Access switch for it.

rules.title: Protected resource used without a usable purpose string
rules.why: iOS shows the purpose string in the permission prompt. A missing key makes the request fail (or the app get rejected); an empty or placeholder text gives users no basis for an informed choice.
rules.fix: Add the Info.plist usage key with a specific sentence that names the feature, such as "Scan a check to deposit it."
rules.verify: Reset privacy settings, trigger the feature, and confirm the prompt shows your specific explanation.

fix_code.code:
<key>NSCameraUsageDescription</key>
<string>Scan the QR code on your card to link it to your account.</string>

rules.title: Entitlement has no matching feature in code
rules.why: Every entitlement widens what the app may reach (HealthKit, App Groups, iCloud, NFC). One the code never uses only adds attack surface and invites App Review questions.
rules.fix: Remove the capability in Xcode's Signing & Capabilities tab, which also deletes the entitlement.
rules.verify: Run `codesign -d --entitlements - MyApp.app` on the archive and confirm the entitlement is gone.

rules.title: Tracking domain isn't declared in the privacy manifest
rules.why: Apple requires apps that track to set NSPrivacyTracking and list tracking domains in NSPrivacyTrackingDomains. Undeclared, the list misleads users, and iOS can't block those hosts when tracking is denied.
rules.fix: Set NSPrivacyTracking to true and add every tracking domain you contact to NSPrivacyTrackingDomains, or stop calling the domain.
rules.verify: Archive the app, generate the privacy report in Xcode's Organizer, and confirm the domain appears under tracking domains.

fix_code.code:
<key>NSPrivacyTracking</key>
<true/>
<key>NSPrivacyTrackingDomains</key>
<array>
    <string>app-measurement.com</string>
</array>

rules.title: App Attest uses the development environment in a release build
rules.why: With appattest-environment set to development, the shipped app requests development attestations, which your server must accept from Apple's sandbox. Any developer-signed copy of the app can then pass.
rules.fix: Set com.apple.developer.devicecheck.appattest-environment to production in the release entitlements.
rules.verify: Check the archived app with `codesign -d --entitlements -` and confirm the value is production.

rules.title: XML parser resolves external entities
rules.why: With external entities or DTD loading on, a crafted XML document can make the parser read local files or send requests to other hosts (XXE), and nested entities can exhaust memory.
rules.fix: Leave shouldResolveExternalEntities false (the default) and drop XML_PARSE_NOENT and XML_PARSE_DTDLOAD from libxml2 options.
rules.verify: Feed the parser a document with `<!ENTITY x SYSTEM "file:///etc/hosts">` and confirm the entity stays unresolved.

rules.title: Sensitive text field lets the keyboard learn what is typed
rules.why: The keyboard learns words typed into fields that aren't secure and keep autocorrection on. A PIN, card number or password typed there can be saved in the keyboard's word list and offered as a suggestion later, to anyone using the phone.
rules.fix: Use isSecureTextEntry = true (SecureField in SwiftUI) for passwords and PINs. For other sensitive fields, set autocorrectionType = .no and spellCheckingType = .no, or .autocorrectionDisabled() in SwiftUI.
rules.verify: Type a test value into the field, then start typing it in Notes. Confirm the keyboard doesn't suggest it.

rules.title: Socket connection sends data without TLS
rules.why: App Transport Security covers URLSession only. A Network.framework connection that uses plain TCP, or a BSD socket or stream to port 80, sends its data in cleartext. Anyone on the same network can read and change it.
rules.fix: Use TLS for the connection: NWParameters(tls:) or .tls for Network.framework, or URLSession for HTTP. Keep plain TCP only for devices on the local network.
rules.verify: Capture the app's traffic with a proxy or packet capture and confirm this connection is TLS, not readable text.

fix_code.code:
let connection = NWConnection(host: "api.example.com", port: .https,
                              using: NWParameters(tls: NWProtocolTLS.Options()))

rules.title: Password field rendered inside a web view
rules.why: A password typed into an HTML input lives in the page's DOM. Any script that runs in the web view, including an injected one, can read it there.
rules.fix: Collect passwords and other secrets with native views (a UITextField with isSecureTextEntry, or a SwiftUI SecureField) placed over the web view, and pass them to your code, not to the page.
rules.verify: Search the HTML the app loads for type="password" and confirm none is left.

rules.title: Secret file is written where backups copy it
rules.why: Files in Documents and Library go into iCloud and computer backups unless they are excluded. A token, key or password file then leaves the device, and it can come back on a different phone.
rules.fix: Keep secrets in the Keychain with a ThisDeviceOnly class. If a file must hold one, set isExcludedFromBackup = true on the file's URLResourceValues after you write it.
rules.verify: Make an unencrypted computer backup of a test device and confirm the file isn't in it.

rules.title: A host the app calls isn't in NSPinnedDomains
rules.why: NSPinnedDomains pins only the hosts it lists, and NSIncludesSubdomains covers one subdomain level. Requests to any other host accept every publicly trusted certificate, so an attacker with a wrongly issued certificate for that host can read them.
rules.fix: Add every host that carries user data or tokens to NSPinnedDomains, with a backup pin. List deeper subdomains on their own. If a host is deliberately unpinned, write down why.
rules.verify: Run the app through a proxy whose CA the test device trusts, and confirm requests to this host fail.
rules.not_needed_reason: Book §8.8: outside banking, health, identity, and apps that handle card numbers, strict TLS plus Certificate Transparency monitoring is a reasonable position, and pinning adds operational risk.
